message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and obligations that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. While this list is comprehensive, it is not exhaustive; you may want to consult a local attorney or tenant‑rights organization for specific questions. | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |----------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may charge a **maximum of one month’s rent** for a security deposit.
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written lease and a copy of the deposit receipt.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the deposit is withheld. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The landlord must repair or replace broken fixtures, appliances, and structural elements. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or terminate the lease (see below). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease specifies them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re experiencing hardship. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment, unlawful entry, or noise complaints to the landlord in writing. | | **Landlord Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord may terminate early only for **material breaches** (e.g., non‑payment, illegal activity). | • Provide written notice and keep copies. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a habitability issue within a reasonable time, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, provided you follow the proper procedure. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and the amount deducted. | | **Rent Increase** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord must give **30 days’ written notice** before raising rent.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent is fixed for the term unless the lease allows increases. | • Review the lease and state law; negotiate if possible. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Eviction** | • The landlord must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• The landlord cannot evict you without a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly; consider legal counsel if you receive an eviction notice. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot surveil tenants without consent (e.g., installing cameras inside the unit). | • Report any unauthorized surveillance to the landlord or local authorities. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the service. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord approval. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are typically responsible for renter’s insurance. | • Consider obtaining coverage for personal property and liability. | --- #### Practical Steps to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** - Look for clauses on rent, security deposit, repairs, entry, and termination. - Verify that any “reasonable notice” periods match Texas law (usually 24–48 hrs for entry, 30 days for rent increases or lease termination). 2. **Document Everything** - Keep a written record of all communications with the landlord (emails, texts, letters). - Take photos or videos of any maintenance issues before reporting them. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** - For repairs: give the landlord a written notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem. - For rent increases or lease termination: provide 30 days’ written notice. 4. **Use the Repair‑and‑Deduct Option Wisely** - Only use this if the landlord fails to act within a reasonable time. - Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the repair and deduction. 5. **Seek Legal Help Early** - If the landlord violates your rights (e.g., unlawful entry, failure to repair, discrimination), consult a tenant‑rights organization or attorney. - In many Texas cities, there are free or low‑cost legal aid services for tenants. 6. **Know Your Local Ordinances** - Some Texas cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas, Houston) have additional tenant protections, such as rent‑control measures, eviction moratoria, or mandatory mediation. - Check your city’s housing department website for local rules. --- #### Quick Reference: When to Call the Landlord | Issue | Typical Timeframe to Notify | Action | |-------|----------------------------|--------| | Broken heating or hot water | Immediately | Written notice; request repair | | Pest infestation | Within 48 hrs | Written notice; request pest control | | Unreasonable noise or harassment | As soon as possible | Written notice; document incidents | | Landlord entry without notice | Immediately | Document entry; request proper notice next time | | Rent increase | 30 days before change | Review lease; negotiate if needed | --- #### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – Chapter 24 (Residential Landlord‑Tenant Law) - **Texas Commission on Human Rights** – Fair Housing complaints - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – Fair Housing hotline - **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid clinics) - **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** – Landlord‑tenant guidance --- **Bottom line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment, and protection against unlawful eviction or discrimination. Keep your lease, document all interactions, and know the statutory notice requirements. If you encounter problems, you can often resolve them through written communication, but you also have legal recourse if the landlord violates your rights.
